372.title: The silver cup (Genesis 44)
372.hook: Judah, who once sold Joseph, offers himself in Benjamin's place
372.howItsDone: Some Christians read Judah's offer as a picture of substitution, someone giving himself in another's place, and preachers set it beside Jesus's death; Matthew 1 traces Jesus's line through Judah.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Simeon held in Egypt, brothers admitting their guilt, and a governor who turned away and wept.

The grain runs out. Jacob refuses, again and again, to let Benjamin go. Finally Judah steps up: put him in my care, and if I don't bring him back, let me bear the blame forever. In Egypt the governor throws them a feast, seats them in birth order, which unnerves them, and gives Benjamin five times as much. They leave at dawn, sacks full, Simeon free, relieved. Then the governor's steward catches up: one of you has stolen my master's silver cup. So sure it's a mistake, they say, whoever has it shall die. The steward searches, oldest to youngest. The last sack is Benjamin's.
screen: `JUDAH PLEDGES HIMSELF.` → `A FEAST IN BIRTH ORDER.` → `THE CUP IN BENJAMIN'S SACK.`

segments.voice: Joseph planted the cup. It's his last test. The brothers tear their clothes and all go back. Then the governor offers them exactly what they once chose: the thief stays as my slave; the rest of you go home in peace. The old situation, set up again. A favored son of Rachel. A chance to be rid of him, and this time they could even say it wasn't their fault. And Judah steps forward. This is the brother who said, years ago at the pit, let's sell him. Genesis has followed him since: he wronged his daughter-in-law Tamar, and ended up admitting she was more righteous than he. Now he makes a long, careful plea. He tells of their old father, who lost one son of the wife he loved, and whose life is bound up in the boy's life. If the boy doesn't come home, the old man will die. Then, in the King James Bible: "Now therefore, I pray thee, let thy servant abide instead of the lad a bondman to my lord; and let the lad go up with his brethren." "For how shall I go up to my father, and the lad be not with me?" Take me instead. The man who sold one brother into slavery offers himself as a slave to save the other. That is the change the test was looking for. Some Christian readers see in Judah a picture of the one who gives himself in another's place, and note that Matthew's Gospel traces Jesus's family line through Judah.

373.title: I am Joseph (Genesis 45:1–15)
373.hook: he can't hold back: I am your brother, don't be distressed, God sent me ahead
373.howItsDone: Christians often read Joseph's words to his brothers as a picture of forgiveness, and preachers set them beside Jesus's teaching to forgive from the heart (Matthew 18:35).

segments.voice: Yesterday, the silver cup in Benjamin's sack, and Judah, who once sold a brother, saying take me instead.

Judah has just finished speaking. The room is silent: Egyptian servants by the walls, eleven brothers fallen on the ground, an old father far away. And the governor, who has held his face still through three days of custody, a feast, a planted cup and Judah's whole plea, can't hold it anymore. In the King James Bible: "Then Joseph could not refrain himself before all them that stood by him; and he cried, Cause every man to go out from me." The servants file out. The door closes. Now there's only family in the room.
screen: `JUDAH FALLS SILENT.` → `HE CAN'T HOLD IT ANYMORE.` → `EVERYONE OUT.`

segments.voice: He weeps so loudly the Egyptians hear it outside, and the news reaches Pharaoh's house. Then he says it: "I am Joseph; doth my father yet live?" In Hebrew, I am Joseph is just two words, and he has waited years to say them. The brothers can't answer; they are troubled at his presence, the text says. The boy they threw in a pit holds their lives in his hand. So he says, come near to me, and they come closer. "I am Joseph your brother, whom ye sold into Egypt." He doesn't pretend it didn't happen. He names it. And before anyone can say sorry: "Now therefore be not grieved, nor angry with yourselves, that ye sold me hither: for God did send me before you to preserve life." He tells the truth about the wrong, and in the same breath tells them not to be crushed by it. He has had years to decide what this story means, and he has decided God was in it, keeping people alive. That doesn't make what they did good. It means the story isn't only about what they did. He falls on Benjamin's neck and weeps, and kisses all his brothers. Then a quiet line that reaches back to the beginning: "after that his brethren talked with him." Once they could not speak peaceably unto him. Now they talk. Some Christian readers hear in this a picture of the forgiveness they believe God offers: the one who was wronged moves first, names the wrong, and draws people near.

Forgiving doesn't mean trusting again right away, and if you pray, you can ask for help with it.

374.title: Jacob goes down to Egypt (Genesis 46:1–7)
374.hook: the old man hears: fear not, I will go down with you
374.howItsDone: Some Christians turn to God's words to Jacob, "I will go down with thee," when moving, emigrating or facing the end of life, and hear them alongside Jesus's promise in Matthew 28:20 to be with his followers always.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a governor in a cleared room said, I am Joseph, whom ye sold. Your line: I am your brother.

The brothers ride home with Egyptian wagons and tell their father the impossible: Joseph is alive, and governor over all the land of Egypt. The old man's heart goes numb, the text says. He doesn't believe them. Then he sees the wagons Joseph sent to carry him, and something in him wakes up. "It is enough; Joseph my son is yet alive: I will go and see him before I die." But going means leaving. Jacob is old; soon he'll tell Pharaoh he is a hundred and thirty. He'd be moving his whole family to a foreign country, in a famine, at the end of his life.
screen: `JOSEPH IS ALIVE.` → `HIS HEART GOES NUMB.` → `THE WAGONS.`

segments.voice: Jacob sets out, and stops at Beersheba, on the southern edge of the land. His grandfather Abraham planted a tree there. His father Isaac built an altar there. And there's a reason to stop and ask. Years before, in a famine, God had told Isaac: don't go down to Egypt. Now Jacob is about to do it. So he offers sacrifices to the God of his father Isaac, and that night God speaks in a vision, in the King James Bible: "Jacob, Jacob. And he said, Here am I." The same answer Abraham gave on the mountain, and Moses will give at the bush. Then: "fear not to go down into Egypt; for I will there make of thee a great nation: I will go down with thee into Egypt; and I will also surely bring thee up again." It doesn't say this will be easy, or even that he'll come home alive. It says, I'm coming with you, and I'll bring you up again. Jacob will die in Egypt, and his body will be carried home. The great nation will come up out of Egypt generations later, through a sea. Then a tender promise: Joseph shall put his hand upon your eyes. You'll die with your son beside you. So seventy souls go down, the text counts, with their flocks and children. Some Christians hear that promise again in the last line of Matthew's Gospel, where the risen Jesus says he is with his followers always.

375.title: Meant for good (Genesis 50:15–21)
375.hook: you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good
375.carry: fear not, I will nourish you
375.howItsDone: Christians often turn to Genesis 50:20 and Romans 8:28 in times of loss or injustice, and the doctrine of providence is taught in catechisms and confessions across Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches, in differing forms.

segments.voice: Yesterday, hineni: Jacob went down to Egypt with a promise. Your line: I will go with you.

Seventeen years in Egypt. Then Jacob dies with his sons around him, and they carry his body home to Canaan, to be buried with Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, and Leah. A huge funeral procession, Egyptians and all. And on the way back, the brothers start doing math. Dad's gone. Dad was the reason Joseph was kind to us. What if he's been waiting? So they send Joseph a message: before he died, your father told us to tell you, please forgive your brothers. Genesis never records Jacob saying it. Readers have wondered ever since if the brothers made it up.
screen: `JACOB IS BURIED.` → `WHAT IF HE'S BEEN WAITING?` → `A MESSAGE FROM DAD.`

segments.voice: When Joseph hears it, he weeps. Seventeen years of kindness, and they still think he's waiting to strike. The brothers fall down before him one more time: we are your servants. And Joseph says, in the King James Bible: "Fear not: for am I in the place of God?" Revenge isn't his job. Then the sentence the whole Joseph story has been building to: "But as for you, ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good, to bring to pass, as it is this day, to save much people alive." It doesn't say the brothers meant well. It doesn't say the pit was good, or the slavery, or the prison. It says two things were happening in the same events. They meant evil. God meant good. This is what Christians call providence, from the Latin providentia, foresight: the belief that God is at work through history, even through human wrongdoing, toward good. Christians hold it in different ways. Some traditions, many Reformed churches among them, stress that God governs all things, even the hard ones. Others prefer to say God permits evil without willing it, and works good out of it. Joseph's sentence leaves room for both. Paul says something close in Romans: all things work together for good to them that love God. And Joseph ends with care, not theology: fear not, I will nourish you and your little ones. And he comforted them, and spoke kindly to them.

If you pray, you can give thanks for what grew; if you don't, simply notice it.

376.title: Genesis close
376.hook: from a garden to a family in Egypt: God keeps promises through broken people
376.howItsDone: Christians read Genesis as the opening of the whole biblical story; reading plans that go through the Bible in order begin here and run straight on into Exodus.

segments.voice: Yesterday, providence: ye thought evil, but God meant it unto good. Your line: fear not, I will nourish you.

Genesis opens with the whole universe: "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Light, oceans, stars, a garden, two people. Fifty chapters later, it closes on a single box: "So Joseph died, being an hundred and ten years old: and they embalmed him, and he was put in a coffin in Egypt." From the heavens to a coffin. If you read it as a story about people getting things right, it's a strange ending. But Genesis was never that story. For forty-five days we've walked through it together. Today, the whole book in one look.
screen: `IN THE BEGINNING.` → `A COFFIN IN EGYPT.` → `FORTY-FIVE DAYS.`

segments.voice: It began with light and good and very good, with dust that had breath in it, and a garden to tend and keep. Then a serpent's question, and God walking in the cool of the day asking, where are you? Coats of skins, made by God, for people who had just disobeyed. Cain and Abel, and being your brother's keeper. Noah building anyway, a dove with an olive leaf, a rainbow that said never again. Babel, where people tried to make a name for themselves. Then one family. Abraham told to go, not knowing where. Stars to count. Hagar, a slave woman, naming the God who sees her. Strangers at Mamre, and Sarah laughing. Abraham arguing with God for a city. Isaac, laughter. A ram on Moriah. Chesed, Esau and a bowl of stew, Jacob in goat skins, a stairway at Bethel, a wrestling match by a river, a brother who ran. And Joseph: a coat, a pit, a prison, and I am your brother. Look at the people. Liars, schemers, favorites, runaways, brothers who sold a brother. Not one is a saint throughout. And yet the promise God made to Abraham, a family through whom all the families of the earth would be blessed, still stands on the last page. Broken people, kept promises. And Genesis ends leaning forward. Joseph's last words: God will surely visit you, and bring you out of this land; carry my bones with you. Christians and Jews both read Genesis as the beginning, not the whole. The coffin waits for a journey.

377.title: A new king (Exodus 1:8–14)
377.hook: a Pharaoh who didn't know Joseph fears the Hebrews and enslaves them
377.howItsDone: Christians read Exodus as the story of God hearing the cry of the oppressed (Exodus 2:23–25; 3:7), and some churches draw on its opening chapters when they pray about forced labor and trafficking today.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Genesis close: a garden at the start, a coffin in Egypt at the end. Your line: broken people, kept promises.

A new book. Jews call it Shemot, names, after its opening words: these are the names of the sons of Israel who came into Egypt. Christians call it Exodus, the Greek word for the way out. It starts where Genesis left off. Joseph dies. His brothers die. That whole generation dies. And their children are fruitful and multiply, the text says, until the land is filled with them. A family that came down for bread has become a people. Then comes one sentence, and the whole story turns on it.
screen: `SHEMOT: NAMES.` → `EXODUS: THE WAY OUT.` → `A FAMILY BECOMES A PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Now there arose up a new king over Egypt, which knew not Joseph." A generation passes, and someone forgot: the man who saved Egypt from famine, and why these people were here at all. Forgetting makes room for fear. The new king tells his people: these Israelites are more and mightier than we are. Let's deal wisely with them, or if a war comes, they'll join our enemies. It's an old move: call your neighbors a threat, and act before they can do anything. So the Egyptians set taskmasters over them, to wear them down with heavy labor. They build store cities for Pharaoh, Pithom and Raamses. "But the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and grew." The plan backfires, so the oppression tightens. The Egyptians made their lives bitter with hard bondage, in mortar and brick and all kinds of work in the field. Bitter will come back: Exodus later tells Israel to eat the Passover with bitter herbs, and Jews still eat them at the Seder. Notice what Exodus doesn't say. It never names this Pharaoh. Historians have proposed different kings, and some doubt we can place the story in Egyptian records at all. The book seems less interested in which king than in what kind. Exodus is a story of God hearing people who cry out, and it starts with a ruler who didn't remember.

You don't know their names; picture them anyway, tired hands, bricks of their own. If you pray, you can pray for them; if you don't, hold them in mind, and let yourself remember them.

Your line: someone forgot. The story of the way out has begun. Day three hundred seventy-seven, done.

378.title: The midwives (Exodus 1:15–21)
378.hook: Shiphrah and Puah refuse to kill the boys; they feared God more than Pharaoh
378.howItsDone: Christians and Jews tell the story of Shiphrah and Puah as an example of refusing an unjust order, and the two are named in sermons on conscience and courage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Shemot: a new king who knew not Joseph, and lives made bitter with brick and mortar. Your line: someone forgot.

Forced labor hasn't worked; the Israelites keep growing. So the king tries something worse, and quieter. He calls in two midwives, the women who sit with mothers in labor and catch the babies. His order: when you deliver a Hebrew woman, look. If it's a son, kill him. If it's a daughter, let her live. A death at a birth could pass for natural. It's an order given in private by the king of Egypt to two women with no power at all. And the Bible, which never tells us this Pharaoh's name, tells us theirs.
screen: `FORCED LABOR FAILS.` → `A PRIVATE ORDER.` → `IF IT'S A SON, KILL HIM.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "the name of the one was Shiphrah, and the name of the other Puah." Then the sentence that makes them unforgettable: "But the midwives feared God, and did not as the king of Egypt commanded them, but saved the men children alive." Here, that fear isn't panic. It's knowing whose word counts for more than the king's. The king calls them back: why have you let the boys live? They have an answer ready. The Hebrew women aren't like Egyptian women, they say. They're lively; the babies are born before we even get there. Was it true, or a clever excuse? The text doesn't say, and readers, Christian and Jewish, still debate it. What it does say is that God dealt well with them, and gave them households of their own. The Hebrew can be read as Hebrew midwives or as midwives to the Hebrews, so we don't know for certain which people they came from. Some ancient Jewish teachers thought they were Moses's own mother and sister. What we do know is that the story of the way out begins with two women saying no. Not with an army, not with a prophet: with two professionals quietly refusing to do harm. This week was full of people choosing: Judah to stay instead of the boy, Joseph not to take revenge, Jacob to go. And now, at the start of a new book, Shiphrah and Puah choose life.
screen: `SHIPHRAH AND PUAH, BY NAME.` · `THE MIDWIVES FEARED GOD.` · `THE HEBREW WOMEN ARE LIVELY.` · `GOD DEALT WELL WITH THEM.` · then, large: `AND SAVED THE MEN CHILDREN ALIVE.`

segments.voice: Say to yourself the name of someone who refused to go along with something they knew was wrong: a nurse, a teacher, a coworker, a grandparent, a stranger in a story you once heard. Maybe nobody thanked them, or even knew; name them anyway, the way the Bible names Shiphrah and Puah. If you pray, you can give thanks for them; if you don't, honor them in your heart.
The midwives. Shiphrah and Puah, who were ordered by Pharaoh to kill the Hebrew baby boys, feared God, and let them live.
Your line: two women said no. The Bible kept both their names. See you tomorrow.
